extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent practitioners/attorneys, USPTO examiners, and PTAB/ARP panel members (particularly those handling §101 Alice analyses, including AI/ML inventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing §101 patent-eligibility (Alice) analyses under the MPEP framework, with emphasis on when claims (including machine‑learning inventions) are directed to an abstract idea versus integrating that exception into a practical application. Focuses on evaluating claim language, specification support, and case law (Enfish, Alice, Mayo, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step framework (patent-eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Alice, first determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept; if so, search for an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the ineligible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance: 'We must first determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept.' If the claims are directed to an abstract idea, proceed to search for elements or combinations that provide significantly more (Alice, 573 U.S. at 217-18; Mayo). This two-step framing is the backbone of the eligibility analysis and guides use of MPEP §§ 2106.04–.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP Step 2A — Prong One (does the claim recite a judicial exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong One asks: does the claim recite an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon? (MPEP §2106.04(II)(A)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Step 2A Prong One analysis 'requir[es] a claim to recite (i.e., set forth or describe) an abstract idea in Prong One before proceeding to the Prong Two inquiry.' If the claim does not recite a judicial exception under Prong One, do not proceed to Prong Two or Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP Step 2A — Prong Two (integration into a practical application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two asks: does the claim recite additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application? (MPEP §2106.04(II)(A)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only after a determination under Prong One that a judicial exception is recited do you evaluate whether additional elements 'integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.' If, at Prong Two, 'the claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception,' the eligibility analysis concludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP Step 2B — inventive concept (significantly more)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B is a search for an 'inventive concept'—elements or combinations that are 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether additional claim elements provide 'significantly more' than the abstract idea (Alice; Mayo). Consider whether any combination of elements rises to the level of an inventive concept beyond generic computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the character of the claims as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'directed to' inquiry looks to the character of the claims as a whole, not merely whether the claims involve a patent-ineligible concept in isolation (Enfish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve eligibility by isolating individual limitations at a high level of generality—consider how the elements work together to achieve improvements (Enfish, 822 F.3d at 1335–39). Panels/examiners should avoid overly cursory analyses that characterize claims too generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical calculations/concepts are often abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that recite mathematical calculations or mathematical concepts can be abstract ideas under Prong One.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from decision: 'computing ... an approximation of a posterior distribution over possible values of the plurality of parameters' was determined to recite a mathematical calculation—a mathematical concept—and thus an abstract idea. Where a party does not dispute a limitation is an abstract idea, proceed to evaluate additional elements under Prong Two/Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reflecting improvements to computer functionality or another technological field may be patent eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to other technology or technical field, can integrate an abstract idea into a practical application and be patent eligible (Enfish; McRO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim limitations themselves reflect the disclosed improvement (e.g., improving how a machine learning model operates by protecting prior-task performance while learning new tasks). Mere presence of an abstract idea does not preclude eligibility if the claim as a whole embodies a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic linking to a technological environment/field of use is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'generally link[] the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use' are not patent eligible (MPEP §2106.05(h); Affinity Labs; Elec. Power Grp.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (a) merely stating a field-of-use or applying an abstract idea in a conventional technological environment and (b) reciting claim limitations that produce a technological improvement. The former fails Prong Two/Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification assertions alone are insufficient to establish eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in the specification asserting improvements are insufficient, by themselves, to support a patent-eligibility determination absent a subsequent determination that the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement (MPEP §2106.05(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and evaluate specification passages (e.g., claims that 'allow the model to preserve performance on earlier tasks') but require that the claim language actually captures that improvement. Reliance solely on spec assertions without claim-level reflection is inadequate (see Intellectual Ventures I LLC v. Symantec Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate significance of additional elements relative to the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination whether additional elements integrate a judicial exception into a practical application requires evaluating the significance of those elements relative to the invention (MPEP §2106.04(d)(II)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether additional elements are meaningful—do they change how a computer or technology functions—or are they token/additional generic steps? The focus is on whether integration into practical application is demonstrated, not merely reciting extra components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equating machine learning with per se unpatentable algorithms or treating claims as 'generic computer components'
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels/examiners should not categorically exclude AI innovations by equating any machine learning with an unpatentable 'algorithm' or by treating remaining elements as mere 'generic computer components.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision warns against high-level generalization that would render many AI innovations unpatentable. Apply precedent (Enfish, McRO) carefully and explain reasoning when acting sua sponte. Use concrete claim-level analysis rather than broad characterizations of ML.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use §§102, 103, and 112 as the traditional tools to limit patent protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 102 (novelty), 103 (nonobviousness), and 112 (written description/claims) are the traditional and appropriate statutory tools to limit patent protection to its proper scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Panel emphasizes these statutory provisions should be the focus of examination to police improper claims scope; §101 analysis should not be a substitute for robust application of §§102,103,112 where appropriate.
